## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

3	// what retires the re-arm, the grace window and the transport dance — and what
4	// makes a lost hand-off a synchronous, visible failure at the executor instead of
5	// a label event fired into the void.

7	// A TASK NAMES AN ENDPOINT, NEVER A URL. The declaration is vendored verbatim
8	// into every consuming repo, so it must never carry deployment detail or anything
9	// adjacent to a credential: `invocation_endpoint: 'fleet'` names a key, and the
10	// repo's own config maps that key to a URL and to the NAME of the repo Actions
11	// secret holding its token. That indirection is also what replaces the whole
12	// self/fleet apparatus — reach is a property of which endpoint you call, so a
13	// task needing wider access names a different endpoint and nothing else in the
14	// system needs a concept of scope.
15	//
16	// THE PROMPT NAMES ONE ITEM AND CARRIES NO INSTRUCTIONS. Everything
17	// behavior-defining is read by the session from the tracked task files at HEAD;
18	// the prompt says which issue and which nonce, and the session validates both in
19	// code before acting (DESIGN §7).

21	export const DEFAULT_ENDPOINT = 'default';
22	
23	// The endpoint is a ROUTINE'S API TRIGGER — `POST /v1/claude_code/routines/
24	// <trigger-id>/fire` with a per-routine bearer token — which is what Claude Code
25	// on the web actually exposes to an HTTP caller. Three consequences the design's
26	// "a CCR API call" did not spell out, each verified against the routines docs
27	// rather than assumed:
28	//
29	//  - THE BEHAVIOR IS THE ROUTINE'S STORED PROMPT, not ours. `text` reaches the
30	//    session wrapped in a `<routine-fire-payload>` block explicitly labelled
31	//    untrusted, and a routine acts on it only because its own saved prompt says
32	//    to. That is the issue-is-data posture arriving for free at one more hop: our
33	//    payload names an item, and every instruction comes from a stored artifact.

69	  if (!entry.url) return { name, error: `invocation endpoint "${name}" declares no url` };
70	  if (!entry.tokenSecret) return { name, error: `invocation endpoint "${name}" declares no tokenSecret (the NAME of the repo Actions secret holding its token)` };
71	  return { name, url: entry.url, tokenEnv: entry.tokenSecret, headers: { ...DEFAULT_HEADERS, ...(entry.headers ?? {}) } };
72	}
73	
74	// The fire payload: which item, and the nonce that proves this call is the one
75	// the hand-off comment recorded. Prose, not JSON — the field is freeform and
76	// unparsed, so a structured payload would arrive as a literal string — and
77	// deliberately free of instructions, because the routine's stored prompt is what
78	// says how to act on it (see `instructions.md`). The session still validates
79	// the item in code before touching it: a payload labelled untrusted is trusted no
80	// more than a label event was.
81	export const firePayload = ({ repo, item, nonce }) =>
82	  `Claudinite work item: ${repo}#${item.number}. Invocation nonce: ${nonce}.`;
83	
84	// The invoker seam the executor calls, exactly once per item. Failure is DATA,
85	// never a throw, and it comes in two kinds the caller must treat differently:
86	//
87	//   { ok: true, sessionId, sessionUrl }   the routine fired; a session exists
88	//   { ok: false, answered: true, error }  the endpoint ANSWERED and refused —
89	//                                         no session, and the cause is a
90	//                                         configuration fault a retry cannot fix
91	//   { ok: false, answered: false, error } no answer reached us — a timeout, a
92	//                                         dropped connection. The session may or
93	//                                         may not exist, and nothing here may
94	//                                         guess which.
95	export function agentInvoker({ repo, config, env = process.env, fetchImpl = fetch, timeoutMs = 60e3 }) {
96	  return async function invoke({ task, item, nonce }) {
97	    const endpoint = resolveEndpoint(config, task);
98	    // A configuration fault, decided before any call: definite, and no session.
99	    if (endpoint.error) return { ok: false, answered: true, error: endpoint.error };
100	    const token = env[endpoint.tokenEnv];
101	    if (!token) {
102	      // The `required_secrets` posture, applied to the endpoint token: nothing
103	      // fails silently, the task just doesn't work yet, and the item names which
104	      // secret to set (DESIGN §14.7).
105	      return { ok: false, answered: true, error: `the Actions secret \`${endpoint.tokenEnv}\` for invocation endpoint "${endpoint.name}" is not set in this repo` };
106	    }
107	
108	    const payload = { text: firePayload({ repo, item, nonce }) };
109	
110	    // ONE call. No loop, and deliberately no `attempts` knob for anyone to raise.
111	    try {
112	      const res = await fetchImpl(endpoint.url, {
113	        method: 'POST',
114	        headers: {
115	          ...endpoint.headers,
116	          'content-type': 'application/json',
117	          authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
118	          'user-agent': 'claudinite-executor',
119	        },
120	        body: JSON.stringify(payload),
121	        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
122	      });
123	      let json = null;
124	      try { json = await res.json(); } catch { json = null; }
125	      if (res.status >= 200 && res.status < 300) {
126	        return {
127	          ok: true,
128	          sessionId: json?.claude_code_session_id ?? null,
129	          sessionUrl: json?.claude_code_session_url ?? null,
130	        };
131	      }
132	      // A status came back, so the endpoint decided: no session was started, and
133	      // the cause is a token, a URL or a routine — none of which a retry fixes.
134	      return {
135	        ok: false, answered: true,
136	        error: `endpoint "${endpoint.name}" returned ${res.status}${json?.error ? `: ${JSON.stringify(json.error)}` : ''}`,
137	      };
138	    } catch (e) {
139	      // Nothing came back. The request may have landed and started a session, so
140	      // this is the one outcome that must never be retried and never be reported
141	      // as a failure — it is genuinely unknown, and the caller says so on the item.
142	      return { ok: false, answered: false, error: `endpoint "${endpoint.name}" gave no answer: ${e.message}` };
143	    }
144	  };
145	}

1	# Growth — discover local packs (per repo)
2	
3	A weekly reflection on **this repo's own** captured knowledge: knowing the Claudinite packs already available to it, notice when project-specific knowledge is worth organizing into a **new local pack** — and author it. A local operation: it writes only the repo's **own** `.claudinite/local/packs/`, landing through a PR **a human reviews** (unlike [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md), which lands unreviewed where the repo's delivery settings allow; the shared canon stays human-gated too — lifting a local pack up is the central promote task's job). Finding nothing new worth a pack is a perfectly good, common outcome.
4	
5	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue. There is no windowed Context to bind — the opportunity is standing (knowledge that was never organized into a pack, not a recent change), so examine the repo as it is.
6	
7	The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: it opens a PR and **never arms auto-merge**. Extract may land unreviewed because it adds prose or a rule to territory a local pack already owns; a **new pack** ships new `.mjs` conformance checks that run at every Stop and in CI the moment it merges — a check can break CI, so it's reviewed, exactly as the sibling [prose-to-checks-sweep](../prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md) is.
8	
9	## Conventions used in this doc
10	
11	- **GitHub access is MCP-only** (`mcp__github__*`) for issue/PR work; read the repo's own tree from the working checkout (local git), never a cross-repo clone.
12	- **The repo's local packs** are everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename window) — the repo's own packs.
13	- **The available canon packs** are the read-only mounted shelf under `.claudinite/shared/packs/` — what Claudinite already homes for this repo. Knowing the shelf is how you avoid re-creating locally what the canon already covers.
14	
15	## The pipeline
16	
17	### 1. Manifest the repo's own stack
18	
19	Catalogue what this project is built on and how it ships — grounded in its files (dependency/build manifests, lockfiles, toolchain/config, CI and release workflows, packaging/signing scripts, source structure, docs), citing the concrete evidence. Do **not** yet consult the pack shelf or decide anything about packs — this step only observes.
20	
21	**Never infer from "projects like this usually…"; if the repo doesn't show it, it is not in the manifest.** If something is present but appears vestigial or aspirational (declared but unused), include it and say so. Be **comprehensive over concise**: a later step filters and decides, so a true item you omit is lost, while an over-included one is cheaply dropped. When unsure whether something rises to an entry, include it with the `?` flag.
22	
23	Catalogue across **three axes**. Put each item under the single axis that fits best; when it genuinely spans two, place it under the primary and cross-note the other.
24	
25	- **Technologies** — languages and their versions, runtimes, frameworks, build systems, and the major libraries that shape how you write and build here (the load-bearing ones, not every transitive dependency).
26	- **External services / APIs** the project integrates with.

# Growth — discover local packs (per repo)

A weekly reflection on **this repo's own** captured knowledge: knowing the Claudinite packs already available to it, notice when project-specific knowledge is worth organizing into a **new local pack** — and author it. A local operation: it writes only the repo's **own** `.claudinite/local/packs/`, landing through a PR **a human reviews** (unlike [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md), which lands unreviewed where the repo's delivery settings allow; the shared canon stays human-gated too — lifting a local pack up is the central promote task's job). Finding nothing new worth a pack is a perfectly good, common outcome.

You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue. There is no windowed Context to bind — the opportunity is standing (knowledge that was never organized into a pack, not a recent change), so examine the repo as it is.

The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: it opens a PR and **never arms auto-merge**. Extract may land unreviewed because it adds prose or a rule to territory a local pack already owns; a **new pack** ships new `.mjs` conformance checks that run at every Stop and in CI the moment it merges — a check can break CI, so it's reviewed, exactly as the sibling [prose-to-checks-sweep](../prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md) is.

## Conventions used in this doc

- **GitHub access is MCP-only** (`mcp__github__*`) for issue/PR work; read the repo's own tree from the working checkout (local git), never a cross-repo clone.
- **The repo's local packs** are everything under `.claudinite/local/packs/` (the legacy `.claudinite/local_packs/` accepted during the rename window) — the repo's own packs.

## The pipeline

Catalogue what this project is built on and how it ships — grounded in its files (dependency/build manifests, lockfiles, toolchain/config, CI and release workflows, packaging/signing scripts, source structure, docs), citing the concrete evidence. Do **not** yet consult the pack shelf or decide anything about packs — this step only observes.

**Never infer from "projects like this usually…"; if the repo doesn't show it, it is not in the manifest.** If something is present but appears vestigial or aspirational (declared but unused), include it and say so. Be **comprehensive over concise**: a later step filters and decides, so a true item you omit is lost, while an over-included one is cheaply dropped. When unsure whether something rises to an entry, include it with the `?` flag.

Catalogue across **three axes**. Put each item under the single axis that fits best; when it genuinely spans two, place it under the primary and cross-note the other.

- **Technologies** — languages and their versions, runtimes, frameworks, build systems, and the major libraries that shape how you write and build here (the load-bearing ones, not every transitive dependency).

Ground and cite every rule in the project's real files. **Never pad** with speculative best-practice rules the evidence doesn't demonstrate; a rule you can't ground, you don't write — a smaller honest pack beats a padded one. **A thing that listens and counts the laughs.** LaughCounter runs quietly on the
always-on Mac mini in your living room, listens through a USB/webcam mic, detects
when you laugh, counts each laugh, tells your laughs from the TV's, and logs it —
so you can see how much joy your days actually hold. It gets better over time from
a hands-free "I just laughed" whenever it misses one.

Everything runs locally. Your Google speaker keeps working as a Google speaker —
LaughCounter never touches it.

### ⬇️ Download

**[Get the latest macOS app → `LaughCounter.dmg`](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg)** · [all releases](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/releases)

A ready-made build, published automatically on every change to `main` — no Xcode. See [`mac/README.md`](mac/README.md) to install.

---

## What it is

A tiny **native macOS menu-bar app** that uses macOS's **built-in** laughter
detection — so there's **nothing to install** (no Python, no TensorFlow, no
Homebrew), nothing downloaded at runtime, and nothing left behind when you delete
it. Drag it to Applications, approve the mic, and a 😄 with today's count appears
in your menu bar.

Everything about installing, using, and building it lives in
**[`mac/README.md`](mac/README.md)**. For the reasoning behind the architecture —
why a native app, how misses become improvements, and the who-laughed plan — see
**[`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md`](docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md)**.

## Does something like this already exist?

Sort of, but nothing that fits this setup:

- **Manual tap counters** ([LaughMeter](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/laughmeter-happiness-tracker/id6757206708),
  [Laughter Meter](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.wejek.app&hl=en_US)) —
  *you* tap each time. Not automatic.
- **[Giggle Gauge](https://gigglegauge.com/)** — the closest: AI that auto-detects
  laughter, but built around phone apps + wearable pendants and cloud services,
  not an always-on box watching just your living room, and it can't learn from
  your corrections.

So LaughCounter is self-hosted and local, and leans on the **pretrained** classifier
already inside macOS, so you never have to hand-label a training set — and nothing
is ever fetched from the network.

---

## How it works

```
 USB/webcam mic ─► Sound Analysis ─► counter ─► JSONL log ─► menu bar
  (living room)    (built into      (distinct   (metadata     (😄 you
                    macOS)           laughs)     only)         📺 TV)
       │                                            ▲
       └──── "I just laughed" (voice or ⌘L) ────────┘
```

1. **Detection** — Apple's Sound Analysis reports, for each ~3s window, how
   strongly it hears laughter, plus what else it heard (music, dialogue, applause).
2. **Counting** turns that noisy stream into discrete laugh *episodes* — a fit of
   giggles is one laugh, a stray blip is none.
3. **You vs the TV** — a strong produced-audio context attributes the laugh to the
   TV, clean laughter to you. It's a hypothesis, logged with its reasoning, and
   only *your* laughs blip.
4. **Logging** appends one JSON line per laugh (time, length, confidence, origin,
   your feedback label). **No audio is recorded** — ever.
5. **Feedback** — a soft blip tells you it caught one; say **"I just laughed"**
   (or press ⌘L) and it logs the one it missed, blipping twice to confirm.

The app uses only built-in frameworks. Nothing is downloaded, at install time or
after.

---

## Setup on the Mac mini

Download the DMG, drag it to Applications, and approve **Microphone** and **Speech
Recognition** when prompted. Add it to **System Settings → General → Login Items**
to have it start with the Mac.

Full steps — including the first-launch Gatekeeper prompt, the laugh-log format,
and building it yourself — are in **[`mac/README.md`](mac/README.md)**.

---

## The feedback loop (how it gets better)

You don't need it perfect on day one. Two tiny habits improve it:

- **When you laugh and hear a blip** → it caught you, nothing to do.
- **When you laugh and *don't* hear a blip** → say **"I just laughed"** (or ⌘L
  from the menu). The miss is logged as a **false negative** — exactly the example
  the detector most needs.

Near-misses are recorded too: anything clearing a deliberately low bar but not the
counting threshold is logged as a `candidate` (uncounted), so later feedback can be
aligned to a nearby event. Every correction becomes the material to sharpen
detection later — threshold tuning now, a personalised Create ML model eventually —
without you ever labeling a dataset up front.

---

## Privacy

- Runs on your Mac mini; **your audio never leaves it** and your Google speaker is
  untouched. There is **no network access at all** — no model download, no
  telemetry, no sync. Detection and speech recognition are both built into macOS
  and run on-device.

  Delete that folder and it's gone.

  LaughCounter to the living room.

---

```bash
cd mac
bash scripts/build-app.sh     # -> dist/LaughCounter.app
bash scripts/make-dmg.sh      # -> dist/LaughCounter.dmg
```

Requires the Swift toolchain (Xcode Command Line Tools); no third-party packages.

name: Build macOS DMG

# Builds the native LaughCounter.app and packages it into a downloadable .dmg —
# entirely on GitHub's macOS runners, so nobody needs Xcode locally.
#
# This is the CI build for feature branches: every push that touches the app
# produces a downloadable artifact. `main` is owned by release-macos-dmg.yml, which
# builds and publishes the DMG to a GitHub Release — so this excludes `main` to
# avoid a duplicate build.
#
# Signing & notarization (optional): if the following repository secrets are
# set, the .dmg is signed with a Developer ID identity and notarized by Apple,
# so it opens with no Gatekeeper warning. Without them, the build still works
# and produces an ad-hoc-signed .dmg (see mac/README.md "Install"). Requires a
# paid Apple Developer account. (release-macos-dmg.yml uses the same secrets.)
#   MACOS_CERT_P12       base64 of the "Developer ID Application" cert (.p12)
#   MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD  the .p12 export password
#   MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY  e.g. "Developer ID Application: Your Name (TEAMID)"
#   APPLE_ID             Apple ID email for notarization
#   APPLE_TEAM_ID        10-char Team ID
#   APPLE_APP_PASSWORD   app-specific password for that Apple ID

on:
  workflow_dispatch:        # lets you build on demand from the Actions tab
  push:
    branches: ["**", "!main"]
    paths:
      - "mac/**"
      - ".github/workflows/build-macos-dmg.yml"

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: macos-14
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: mac
        shell: bash   # runs steps with `bash -o pipefail` so piped commands fail loudly
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Swift toolchain
        run: swift --version

      # Signing + notarization only run when the repo has the signing secrets
      # configured. Without them the build still succeeds and produces an
      # ad-hoc-signed .dmg (users clear Gatekeeper manually — see mac/README.md).
      - name: Detect signing secrets
        id: signing
        env:
          MACOS_CERT_P12: ${{ secrets.MACOS_CERT_P12 }}
        run: |
          if [ -n "$MACOS_CERT_P12" ]; then
            echo "enabled=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "enabled=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            echo "::notice::No MACOS_CERT_P12 secret set — building an ad-hoc (unnotarized) DMG."
          fi

      - name: Import Developer ID certificate
        if: steps.signing.outputs.enabled == 'true'
        env:
          MACOS_CERT_P12: ${{ secrets.MACOS_CERT_P12 }}
          MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          KEYCHAIN="$RUNNER_TEMP/signing.keychain-db"
          KEYCHAIN_PW="$(uuidgen)"
          security create-keychain -p "$KEYCHAIN_PW" "$KEYCHAIN"
          security set-keychain-settings -lut 21600 "$KEYCHAIN"
          security unlock-keychain -p "$KEYCHAIN_PW" "$KEYCHAIN"
          echo "$MACOS_CERT_P12" | base64 --decode > "$RUNNER_TEMP/cert.p12"
          security import "$RUNNER_TEMP/cert.p12" -k "$KEYCHAIN" \
            -P "$MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD" -T /usr/bin/codesign
          security set-key-partition-list -S apple-tool:,apple: -s -k "$KEYCHAIN_PW" "$KEYCHAIN" >/dev/null
          # Make our keychain searchable alongside the login keychain.
          security list-keychains -d user -s "$KEYCHAIN" \
            $(security list-keychains -d user | sed 's/["[:space:]]//g')
          rm -f "$RUNNER_TEMP/cert.p12"

      - name: Build LaughCounter.app
        env:
          MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY: ${{ steps.signing.outputs.enabled == 'true' && secrets.MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY || '' }}
        run: bash scripts/build-app.sh

      - name: Package .dmg
        run: bash scripts/make-dmg.sh

      - name: Notarize .dmg
        if: steps.signing.outputs.enabled == 'true'

          APPLE_TEAM_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_TEAM_ID }}
          APPLE_APP_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.APPLE_APP_PASSWORD }}
        run: bash scripts/notarize-dmg.sh

      - name: Upload DMG artifact
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: LaughCounter-dmg
          path: mac/dist/LaughCounter.dmg
          if-no-files-found: error

# set, the .dmg is signed with a Developer ID identity and notarized by Apple,

# and produces an ad-hoc-signed .dmg (see mac/README.md "Install"). Requires a
# paid Apple Developer account. (release-macos-dmg.yml uses the same secrets.)
#   MACOS_CERT_P12       base64 of the "Developer ID Application" cert (.p12)
#   MACOS_CERT_PASSWORD  the .p12 export password
#   MACOS_SIGN_IDENTITY  e.g. "Developer ID Application: Your Name (TEAMID)"
#   APPLE_ID             Apple ID email for notarization
#   APPLE_TEAM_ID        10-char Team ID
#   APPLE_APP_PASSWORD   app-specific password for that Apple ID

  workflow_dispatch:        # lets you build on demand from the Actions tab
  push:
    branches: ["**", "!main"]
    paths:

      - ".github/workflows/build-macos-dmg.yml"

permissions:
  contents: read

  build:
    runs-on: macos-14
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: mac
        shell: bash   # runs steps with `bash -o pipefail` so piped commands fail loudly

      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Swift toolchain
        run: swift --version

      # configured. Without them the build still succeeds and produces an
      # ad-hoc-signed .dmg (users clear Gatekeeper manually — see mac/README.md).
      - name: Detect signing secrets
        id: signing
        env:
          MACOS_CERT_P12: ${{ secrets.MACOS_CERT_P12 }}
        run: |
          if [ -n "$MACOS_CERT_P12" ]; then
            echo "enabled=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

            echo "enabled=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            echo "::notice::No MACOS_CERT_P12 secret set — building an ad-hoc (unnotarized) DMG."

98	Laughs are appended to `~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughs.jsonl`,
99	one JSON object per line, fields in a fixed order:
100	
101	| field | meaning |
102	|-------|---------|
103	| `start_iso` | human-readable start time (ISO-8601) |
104	| `label` | `auto` (detected), `missed` (you told us we missed one), `candidate` (sub-threshold — logged for tuning, **not counted**), `rejected` (not counted) |

106	| `peak` | highest laughter confidence during the laugh (0–1, rounded) |
107	| `duration` | `end − start` in seconds. **Coarse:** the built-in classifier analyses in ~3s windows, so a single laugh reads ~3s; only laughs spanning several windows read longer. It's a rough length, not a precise one. |
108	| `mean` | average laughter confidence across the laugh |
109	| `source` | `mic` (auto), `voice` (spoken “I just laughed”), `button` (menu / ⌘L) |
110	| `origin` | you-vs-TV **hypothesis**: `me` or `tv` |
111	| `tv_signal` | strongest produced-audio context (0–1) the hypothesis is based on |
112	| `origin_reason` | plain-language why (e.g. `music=0.66 (soundtrack/audience) → TV`) |
113	| `type` | which laugh class fired (e.g. giggle, chuckle), when known |
114	| `context` | top competing non-laugh classes heard |
115	
116	**You vs the TV (two counters).** The menu bar shows `😄 N  📺 M` — your laughs vs
117	the TV's, today. Each laugh gets a *hypothesis*, not a verdict: a strong
118	produced-audio context (music, dialogue, audience, instruments — `tv_signal ≥ 0.3`)
119	is attributed to the TV; clean laughter with little of that is attributed to you.
120	Only *your* laughs blip. It will guess wrong sometimes (a real laugh over TV music),
121	which is why every laugh is still logged with its reasoning — nothing is discarded.
122	The class-based classifier can't hear *who* laughed; a loudness/proximity signal and,
123	eventually, laugh enrollment would sharpen it.
124	
125	**Sub-threshold logging:** anything that clears a deliberately low bar but not the
126	counting threshold is written with `label:"candidate"` (uncounted) — so near-misses
127	are on record and later “I laughed” feedback can be aligned to a nearby event.
128	
129	**Which build am I running?** The menu's first line carries it —
130	`LaughCounter v0.3.2 (6)`. The number in brackets is the build: two DMGs can share
131	a version string when a change ships without a version bump, and the build number
132	is what tells them apart.
133	
134	**Pause:** *Pause listening* (⌘P) stops counting and hands the microphone back
135	until you pick *Start listening* again — the menu shows `Status: paused` meanwhile.
136	It isn't remembered across launches: quitting and reopening starts it listening
137	again, which is what an always-on box should do after a power cut.
138	
139	**Sleep, standby & the sleeping display:** the mic is released when the Mac sleeps
140	and picked back up when it returns. It resumes **only if the counter was running
141	when the Mac went to sleep**: sleep it while paused, or with the microphone never
142	granted, and it comes back off. A wake with nobody there (Power Nap, a screensaver
143	dismissed) doesn't restart anything that was already running.
144	
145	A **USB webcam mic can also disappear while the display sleeps** — macOS tears the
146	input device down and it only comes back when the display wakes. Counting pauses
147	for that whole window; there is nothing the app can do about it beyond noticing
148	and recovering. It keeps checking once a minute and picks up automatically the
149	moment the device returns, so the only sign is a gap in the log (and one
150	`input device still unavailable` line, not a line a minute). If you want counting
151	to continue through a long film, stop the *display* from sleeping — System
152	Settings → Lock Screen → *Turn display off* — since *Keep Mac awake while
153	listening* deliberately allows display sleep.
154	
155	**Activity log:** lifecycle events (started / slept / woke / reconfigured / errors)
156	and each laugh's hypothesis go to `laughcounter.log` next to the laugh log (open it
157	from the menu), so if listening ever stops — or a guess looks off — you can see why.
158	
159	## Notes & limits
160	
161	See [`../docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md`](../docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md) for the
162	full picture: how misses become improvements (threshold tuning now, a personalised
163	Create ML model later), the who-laughed plan, and the voice-command tradeoffs
164	(false triggers, on-device availability).

| `context` | top competing non-laugh classes heard |

**You vs the TV (two counters).** The menu bar shows `😄 N  📺 M` — your laughs vs
the TV's, today. Each laugh gets a *hypothesis*, not a verdict: a strong
produced-audio context (music, dialogue, audience, instruments — `tv_signal ≥ 0.3`)
is attributed to the TV; clean laughter with little of that is attributed to you.
Only *your* laughs blip. It will guess wrong sometimes (a real laugh over TV music),
which is why every laugh is still logged with its reasoning — nothing is discarded.
The class-based classifier can't hear *who* laughed; a loudness/proximity signal and,
eventually, laugh enrollment would sharpen it.

**Sub-threshold logging:** anything that clears a deliberately low bar but not the
counting threshold is written with `label:"candidate"` (uncounted) — so near-misses
are on record and later “I laughed” feedback can be aligned to a nearby event.

**Which build am I running?** The menu's first line carries it —
`LaughCounter v0.3.2 (6)`. The number in brackets is the build: two DMGs can share
a version string when a change ships without a version bump, and the build number
is what tells them apart.

**Pause:** *Pause listening* (⌘P) stops counting and hands the microphone back
until you pick *Start listening* again — the menu shows `Status: paused` meanwhile.
It isn't remembered across launches: quitting and reopening starts it listening
again, which is what an always-on box should do after a power cut.

**Sleep, standby & the sleeping display:** the mic is released when the Mac sleeps
and picked back up when it returns. It resumes **only if the counter was running
when the Mac went to sleep**: sleep it while paused, or with the microphone never
granted, and it comes back off. A wake with nobody there (Power Nap, a screensaver
dismissed) doesn't restart anything that was already running.

A **USB webcam mic can also disappear while the display sleeps** — macOS tears the
input device down and it only comes back when the display wakes. Counting pauses
for that whole window; there is nothing the app can do about it beyond noticing
and recovering. It keeps checking once a minute and picks up automatically the
moment the device returns, so the only sign is a gap in the log (and one
`input device still unavailable` line, not a line a minute). If you want counting
to continue through a long film, stop the *display* from sleeping — System
Settings → Lock Screen → *Turn display off* — since *Keep Mac awake while
listening* deliberately allows display sleep.

**Activity log:** lifecycle events (started / slept / woke / reconfigured / errors)
and each laugh's hypothesis go to `laughcounter.log` next to the laugh log (open it
from the menu), so if listening ever stops — or a guess looks off — you can see why.

See [`../docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md`](../docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md) for the
full picture: how misses become improvements (threshold tuning now, a personalised

on-device-privacy boundary. That boundary is the product's defining constraint and keeps its own
pack (`local/on-device-privacy`, checks included); this one is where everything else lands so it
